stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Paleobotanists working in the shale deposits of a former Eocene lake have recovered hundreds of exceptionally preserved plant fossils. The fossilized leaves from the site's lowest layer, which include a nearly complete frond of an extinct tree fern, ______ that the surrounding landscape once supported a warm, humid forest rather than the dry scrubland found there today.
explanation: The subject of the main clause is "leaves," and nothing after it is a main verb yet. The "which" clause already has its own verb ("include"), so it doesn't count. That means the blank needs a finite verb. Because "leaves" is plural, the verb has to be the plural "suggest."

A.why: You matched the verb to "fern" or "frond," the singular nouns just before the blank. Cross out the "which" clause and you're left with "the fossilized leaves... suggests," which is a number mismatch.

C.why: "Suggesting" reads smoothly, but an -ing form can't serve as a main verb. With it, "leaves" never gets a tensed verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

D.why: An infinitive can't serve as a sentence's main verb. "The fossilized leaves... to suggest that" leaves the subject without a predicate.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In the summer of 1841, the county hired surveyor Adela Voss to produce its first reliable map. Over eleven weeks, Voss walked the full length of the Marrow River valley with a measuring chain and a brass compass and ______ every bend of the river, each mill site, and each ford in a leather field notebook. Those notes remained the basis of the county's official maps for nearly a century.
explanation: The "and" before the blank joins two actions that Voss performed. The first one is "walked," a finite past-tense verb. The second action has to be parallel to it, so it also has to be a finite past-tense verb: "Voss walked... and recorded."

A.why: You read "recording" as a description of how she walked. After "and," though, the blank is the second half of a compound predicate. It needs a tensed verb parallel to "walked," not a participle.

B.why: "To record" sounds like it gives the purpose of the walk, but "walked... and to record" uses "and" to join a finite verb to an infinitive. That isn't parallel.

D.why: "Having recorded" is a nonfinite perfect participle. It can't be the second main verb after "and," and it also suggests the recording happened before the walking.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most eighteenth-century broadsides were printed cheaply and discarded within days, so few examples remain. Printed from a single pearwood block in just two colors, the illustrated ballad sheet that two apprentices in a Leiden workshop pulled from the press in 1784 ______ in only three known impressions, one of which is now held by a museum in Amsterdam.
explanation: The opening modifier describes "the illustrated ballad sheet," which is the subject. The verb "pulled" belongs to the "that" clause, so the sheet still has no main verb of its own. The blank needs a finite verb, and since "sheet" is singular, that verb is "survives."

B.why: You matched the verb to "apprentices," the plural noun inside the "that" clause. The subject is the singular "sheet," so the plural "survive" doesn't agree.

C.why: You may have counted "pulled" as the sentence's main verb. It belongs to the "that" clause, though. "Surviving" leaves "sheet" without a tensed verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

D.why: "Having survived" is a participle and can't be a main verb. The subject "sheet" still never gets a predicate.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: When the city of Harlow adopted its first zoning code in 1962, planners were responding to decades of factories crowded beside tenements. The code, which ______ homes, shops, and workshops onto separate parcels across the city, was replaced in 2019 by a form-based code that regulates the shape and placement of buildings rather than their use.
explanation: The main clause already has its verb, since "The code... was replaced." The blank sits inside the "which" clause, and a relative clause needs its own finite verb. The code was in force in the past, so the past-tense "segregated" completes the clause.

A.why: "The code, segregating homes..." would work without "which." With "which" there, the clause needs a tensed verb, and "which segregating" is a fragment.

B.why: "To segregate" sounds like the code's purpose. An infinitive can't be the verb of a "which" clause, though, so the clause is left with no predicate.

C.why: "Having segregated" is a participle, not a finite verb. The "which" clause still has no verb of its own.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Economists have long debated whether minimum-wage increases cost workers their jobs. A 2021 analysis of payroll records from more than 4,000 small restaurants and retailers across six states ______ that higher wage floors reduced employee turnover by nearly a fifth, a saving the authors argue offset much of the added labor cost for employers.
explanation: Cross out the prepositional phrases ("of payroll records," "from more than 4,000 small restaurants and retailers," "across six states"). What's left is the singular subject "A 2021 analysis," and it has no main verb yet. The blank needs a finite verb that agrees with "analysis," which is "indicates."

A.why: You matched the verb to "retailers" or "states," the plural nouns just before the blank. The subject is the singular "analysis," so the plural "indicate" doesn't agree.

B.why: An infinitive can't be a main verb. "A 2021 analysis... to indicate that" leaves the subject without a predicate.

C.why: "Indicating" sounds complete if you read quickly, but an -ing form isn't a tensed verb. The sentence ends up with no main verb, so it's a fragment.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a hillside settlement in southern Portugal uncovered a cluster of storage pits dug roughly 5,000 years ago. Most held only ash, but one stood apart. The largest pit, which contained charred barley, several broken loom weights, and a bone comb that researchers believe was used to prepare wool fibers, ______ the strongest evidence yet that the settlement's residents processed grain and textiles in a single shared workspace.
explanation: Strip out the long relative clause ("which contained ... wool fibers") and you are left with "The largest pit ______ the strongest evidence yet." The subject "pit" has no main verb yet. The verbs inside the clause ("contained," "believe," "was used") belong to that clause, not to "pit." Only a finite verb can finish the sentence, and the singular present-tense "provides" agrees with "pit."

A.why: "Providing" sounds fluent after such a long clause, but an -ing form can't serve as a main verb. You probably counted "contained" or "believe" as the sentence's verb. They both sit inside the relative clause, so "pit" is left without a verb and the sentence is a fragment.

B.why: "To provide" reads like a statement of the pit's purpose, but an infinitive isn't a tensed verb. The subject "pit" would still have no main verb.

D.why: "Having provided" looks like a past action because of "having," but it is a participle, not a finite verb. You may have taken it for "has provided." Without "has," the sentence has no main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Memory B cells are long-lived immune cells that remain in the body after an infection has cleared, sometimes for decades. They do little while the threat is absent. If the same pathogen returns, however, these cells, which have already been tuned to recognize its surface proteins, rapidly multiply and ______ large quantities of matching antibodies, a response that can begin within days rather than the weeks a first infection requires.
explanation: The subject "these cells" has a compound predicate joined by "and." The first verb is "multiply," which is finite and in the present tense. The verb after "and" must be parallel to it, so you need the finite present-tense "secrete": the cells "multiply and secrete" antibodies.

A.why: "Secreting" would work after a comma ("multiply, secreting antibodies"), but after "and" it has to match "multiply." Joining a finite verb to an -ing form with "and" breaks the parallel structure.

C.why: You may have read "to secrete" as the reason the cells multiply. With "and" in front of it, though, it has to be the second verb of the predicate, and an infinitive isn't parallel to "multiply."

D.why: "Having secreted" is a nonfinite perfect participle. It doesn't match "multiply" in form, and it also puts the secreting before the multiplying, which reverses the order of events in the passage.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Patented in France in 1804, the Jacquard loom automated the weaving of intricate patterns such as brocade and damask. The loom read a long chain of stiff pasteboard cards, each punched with a grid of holes. Every card in the chain, which could run to thousands of cards for a single large design, ______ which of the warp threads would be lifted for one pass of the shuttle.
explanation: Cross out "in the chain" and the clause "which could run ... large design." What's left is "Every card ______ which of the warp threads would be lifted." "Every card" is the subject, and it doesn't have a main verb yet. "Could run" belongs to the which-clause, and "would be lifted" belongs to the noun clause after the blank. The passage is set in the past, so the finite past-tense "determined" completes the sentence.

A.why: "Determining" sounds natural after the long interruption. You probably treated "could run" or "would be lifted" as the main verb, but neither one belongs to "Every card," so the sentence is left as a fragment.

C.why: "To determine" states a purpose. It isn't a tensed verb, so the subject "Every card" still has no main verb.

D.why: "Having determined" is a participle. It can describe a noun, but it can't serve as the main verb that "Every card" needs.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In 2018, the council of a midsize river city adopted a plan to convert downtown's surface parking lots, most of which sat empty after business hours, into apartment buildings with shops on the ground floor. Critics warned that the loss of parking would drive visitors away. Instead, the plan, together with a new bus line linking the former lots to outlying neighborhoods, ______ the number of people living within a ten-minute walk of the transit center.
explanation: The subject of the last sentence is "the plan." "Together with a new bus line ..." is an interrupter and doesn't add to the subject. Nothing finite follows "the plan," because "linking" is a participle that describes "bus line." The sentence needs a finite verb, and "Instead" contrasts with the critics' past-tense prediction, so the simple past "nearly doubled" fits.

A.why: "Nearly doubling" echoes "linking" just before the blank, so it sounds smooth. However, two -ing forms still leave "the plan" without a main verb, and the sentence becomes a fragment.

C.why: Earlier in the passage the writer says "a plan to convert," so "to nearly double" can sound like another description of the plan's goal. Here, though, it leaves the subject without a tensed verb. It would also turn a reported result into a mere intention.

D.why: "Having nearly doubled" is a nonfinite participle. You may have read it as "has nearly doubled," but without "has" it can't be the main verb for "the plan."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Volcanic ash can preserve plants in extraordinary detail because it buries them quickly and seals out oxygen. At one fossil site, falling ash covered an entire forest floor about 298 million years ago. A single fern frond recovered there, along with the dozens of spore capsules still clustered on its underside, ______ paleobotanists to reconstruct, in unusual detail, how the plant reproduced.
explanation: The subject is "A single fern frond." "Recovered there" is a participle modifying it. "Along with the dozens of spore capsules ..." is an interrupter, and "along with" doesn't make a subject plural. That leaves a singular subject with no main verb, so you need a finite singular verb: "has allowed."

A.why: "Allowing" sounds fluent, but it's an -ing form, and the only other verb nearby, "recovered," is a participle too. The subject "frond" is left with no main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.why: You correctly chose a finite verb, but you matched it to "capsules," the plural noun just before the blank, or you treated "along with" as if it meant "and." The real subject, "frond," is singular and needs "has allowed."

D.why: "To allow" is an infinitive, not a tensed verb. You may have heard it as a statement of purpose, but the subject "frond" still has no main verb.
